A. Standard formulation

Data can come from files, SQL databases, automatic logs, machine recordings, binary streams, etc. For data mining, we put it into a standard mathematical form.
TermMeaningExam wording
Universe of objectsall objects of interest, usually very largewe observe only a small part
Attribute / variablea property describing an objectfeature / column
Record / instancevalues of variables for one objectrow / example
Datasetcomplete data available for an applicationusually a table of instances

B. Labelled vs unlabelled

Labelled data
One attribute has special significance and the aim is to predict it.
Example: MNIST image + digit label; spam/not spam.
Unlabelled data
No specially designated target attribute.
Example: Netflix-style user/movie behaviour before a target is chosen.
Trap: labelled/unlabelled is about whether there is a target to predict, not whether columns have names.
09.05.2026Lecture 2 - instance-based vs model-based

C. Instance-based vs model-based learning

Instance-based learning
The system learns examples “by heart”. For a new item, it compares the item with stored examples using similarity/distance.
Local generalisation; kNN is the key later example.
Model-based learning
Build a model/function from examples, then use the model to make predictions.
More compact and portable than carrying the full dataset.

Recording 3 emphasis

The lecturer stresses that prediction assumes the past is a useful indicator of the future. Instance-based: compare every new object with data already stored. Weakness: huge datasets make comparison and storage expensive. Model-based: learn a function/model, then prediction is faster and does not require shipping the whole dataset.
Exam sentence: instance-based learning keeps training examples and uses similarity at prediction time; model-based learning compresses experience into a learned function/model.
09.05.2026Lecture 2 - formal learning framework

D. Formal Learning Framework - Exam Ready

Correct full framework

Exam-ready version:
We are given training examples , sampled from an unknown generating process . We choose a hypothesis space , the class of possible decision functions. For , the loss function measures the error of on example . The ideal aim is to minimise the expected loss , but since is unknown, in practice we minimise the empirical average loss over the training data.

The one thing to memorise

Training sample
Unknown source
Random example
Candidate decision function
Loss on random example
Average future error
Training average
Exam trap: do not stop at “learns from data”. Say what the sample is, what the unknown source is, what functions are allowed, what the loss measures, and why empirical loss replaces expected loss.
09.05.2026Lecture 2 - supervised and unsupervised learning

E. Supervised / Unsupervised Learning in the Framework

Supervised learning

Each example is an input-target pair: z=(x,y). The function f takes x as input and predicts y or a distribution over y.
Regression loss
Use when y is real-valued, e.g. a scalar/vector target.
Classification negative log-likelihood
Use when y is a finite class index and f_i(x) estimates P(y=i|x).

Unsupervised learning

There is no target label y. The function f helps describe the unknown distribution P(Z). Sometimes f estimates P(Z) directly: density estimation. Often f describes where the density concentrates: clustering. Hard clustering gives each point one cluster, e.g. k-means. Soft clustering gives probabilities of cluster membership, e.g. Gaussian mixture models. Another unsupervised goal is learning a new representation of Z.

Ockham's razor

Memorise: Ockham’s razor says we prefer the simplest hypothesis consistent with the data. This is a model-selection principle: among functions that fit the data, prefer the simpler one.

Main steps of data mining from Lecture 2

Step 1: represent data in standard form. Step 2: define distance/similarity measures for finding similar items. The lecture calls this local generalisation. Step 3: apply algorithms such as kNN, Naive Bayes, k-means, PageRank, SVM, AdaBoost, EM, and graph mining algorithms.
09.05.2026Lecture 2 - softmax and cross entropy

F. Softmax + Cross Entropy

Softmax function

Softmax takes any K-dimensional vector of real scores and returns K numbers between 0 and 1 that add up to 1.
Map
Formula
It is a generalisation of the logistic function. Its output can represent a categorical distribution over K possible outcomes.
Exam wording: softmax squashes arbitrary real-valued class scores into class probabilities.

Cross entropy

Cross entropy measures the average number of bits needed to identify an event drawn from the true distribution p if we use a coding scheme optimised for q instead.
Information-theory definition
Discrete case
Here H(p) is the entropy of p. DKL(p||q) is the Kullback-Leibler divergence.
Common mistake: cross entropy is not “accuracy”. It is a loss/uncertainty measure comparing probability distributions.
09.05.2026Lecture 2 - softmax exam wording

Softmax: Exam-Ready Wording

Definition and interpretation

The softmax function converts a vector of real-valued class scores into a probability distribution over classes. The exponential makes all entries positive, and division by the sum normalises them so that the outputs add to 1. Therefore can be interpreted as an estimate of .
Softmax formula
09.05.2026Lecture 2 - cross entropy exam wording

Cross Entropy: Exam-Ready Classification Wording

Cross entropy

Cross entropy measures the difference between two probability distributions and over the same set of events.
Discrete cross entropy

What it means in classification

In classification, is the true distribution and is the model’s predicted distribution. For one MNIST image whose true digit is 2, the true distribution is basically one-hot: If the true class is , cross entropy becomes the negative log probability assigned to the correct class:
Classification loss
Interpretation: the loss is small when the model assigns high probability to the correct class, and large when it assigns low probability to the correct class.
Common mistake: softmax produces probabilities; cross entropy is the loss used to judge those probabilities against the true label.

09.05.2026Lecture 2 - TF-IDF intuition and formulas

G. TF-IDF + Vector Space Model

Textual data preparation

Text mining often begins with documents and automatically extracted features. Typical preparation: words/sentences extraction, removing stop words, and stemming. There are usually many features; many occur rarely; many can be noisy or irrelevant.

Why frequency alone is wrong

The lecture warns that the most frequent words in a document are not usually the best topic indicators. Useful topic words are often relatively rare across the whole corpus but concentrated in a few documents.
Memorise the “albeit/chukker” idea: some rare words are not useful because they are scattered and do not indicate a topic; a word such as “chukker” is useful because if it appears once in a polo article, it is likely to appear repeatedly in that same topic-specific document.

Definitions

Term frequency
Normalise by the most frequent term in document j.
Inverse document frequency
Large for words appearing in few documents.
TF-IDF score
High score = frequent in this document but rare/concentrated in the corpus.

Bound proof pattern for past papers

General bound
Because TF≤1 and n_i≥1.
2023-style 500 docs
2024-style 1500 docs
Exam sentence: the largest possible IDF occurs when the word appears in only one document, so IDF = log₂(N); TF cannot exceed 1; therefore TF-IDF cannot exceed log₂(N).

Fast calculation memory

First compute IDF from the whole corpus: N and n_i. Then compute TF inside the particular document: count of word divided by maximum word count in that document. Multiply TF by IDF.
Common mistake: do not divide by the total number of words in the document. Lecture 2 defines TF using the maximum term frequency in that document.

P4 - TF-IDF with 2048 documents

09.05.2026Lecture 2 - Tutorial 1 P5 worked solution

Tutorial 1 P5: Worked Solution

This is the official solution logic for converting the document-term matrix into a TF-IDF matrix.

Step 1 - clean the matrix

Remove all-zero columns/rows as instructed in the official solution. Here, document D7 is removed because it is an all-zero column.

Step 2 - compute TF column by column

For each remaining document column, divide every count by the largest count in that column. Example: in D3 the maximum count is 8, so entries 1 and 8 become 1/8 and 1.

Step 3 - compute IDF row by row

There are 7 remaining documents, so each row gets IDF = log₂(7/Nᵢ).

H. Graph theory: compact lecture glossary

Exam purpose: recognise graph vocabulary fast, then use it in Tutorial 1 P6-P9: degree theorem, adjacency matrices, and walks.
Lecture 2 example
Left: undirected graph. Right: directed graph. In the lecture example, the left graph has |V|=8 and |E|=11.
Graph vs edge types
TermLecture 2 meaning to memorise
GraphG=(V,E): V is a finite nonempty set of vertices/nodes; E is a set of edges.
Edge / loop / simple graphAn edge joins vertices. A loop is (v_i,v_i). A simple graph is undirected and has no loops.
Incident / adjacent / neighboursIf e=(v_i,v_j), then e is incident with v_i and v_j. The vertices are adjacent/neighbours, written v_i ~ v_j.
Order / sizeOrder = |V| = n, the number of vertices. Size = |E| = m, the number of edges.
Directed graph / arcA directed graph has ordered pairs of vertices. A directed edge (v_i,v_j) is an arc from tail v_i to head v_j.
Weighted graphA weight w_ij is attached to edge (v_i,v_j), often representing cost, length or capacity. Weights are strictly positive.
09.05.2026Lecture 2 - graph theory: degree, path and distance

Degree, walk, path, cycle, shortest path and distance

Exam purpose: these are definition marks and they also support Tutorial 1 P8, where powers of the adjacency matrix count walks.
One graph for all route definitions
Degree in one line
Undirected: d(vᵢ) = number of edges incident with vᵢ. Directed: id(vᵢ) counts incoming arcs; od(vᵢ) counts outgoing arcs. Theorem: in an undirected graph, ∑v∈Vdeg(v)=2|E|.
Reason: every edge touches two endpoints, so it is counted twice in the total degree sum.
TermLecture 2 meaningQuick example from the picture
WalkOrdered sequence x=v₀,v₁,...,vₜ=y where every consecutive pair is joined by an edge. Vertices and edges may repeat.A,B,C,B,E is a walk.
LengthNumber of hops/edges used; it is t, not the number of vertices listed.A,B,C,D has length 3.
Closed walkA walk that starts and ends at the same vertex.B,C,E,B is closed.
TrailA walk with distinct edges. Vertices may repeat.A,B,C,E,B can be a trail if no edge repeats.
PathA walk with distinct vertices, except possibly the start/end vertex when discussing cycles.A,B,C,D is a path.
CycleA closed path of length t ≥ 3; it begins and ends at the same vertex and has distinct nodes around the cycle.B,C,E,B is a cycle.
Shortest pathA path of minimum length between two nodes.A-B-E is shorter than A-B-C-E.
DistanceThe length of the shortest path, written d(x,y). If no path exists, d(x,y)=∞.d(A,E)=2.
Common exam trap: a walk is the loosest object; it can repeat. A path is stricter. Distance is not any path length, but the minimum path length.

09.05.2026Lecture 2 - graph theory: connectedness and adjacency matrix

Connectedness, components, strong/weak connection, adjacency matrix

Connected components
Weakly vs strongly connected directed graphs
TermLecture 2 meaningExam wording
Connected nodesTwo nodes are connected if there exists a path between them.Find a path; if one exists, they are connected.
Connected graphA graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices.Every vertex can reach every other vertex.
Connected componentA maximal connected subgraph.A largest separate connected piece; you cannot add more vertices to it without losing connectedness.
Strongly connectedFor a directed graph, there is a directed path between all ordered pairs of vertices.For every u and v, you need u→v and v→u by directed paths.
Weakly connectedFor a directed graph, paths exist only after treating directed edges as undirected.Ignore arrow directions, then check connectedness.
Adjacency matrix picture
Adjacency matrix rules
Binary: A(i,j)=1 if vᵢ is adjacent to vⱼ, otherwise 0. Undirected: A is symmetric. Directed: A need not be symmetric, because (vᵢ,vⱼ) does not imply (vⱼ,vᵢ). Weighted: A(i,j)=wᵢⱼ if vᵢ is adjacent to vⱼ, otherwise 0.
Exam link: in Tutorial 1 P8, (Aʳ)(i,j) counts walks of length r from vᵢ to vⱼ.

Degree sum theorem
Each undirected edge contributes 1 to the degree of each endpoint.

Tutorial 1 P7 - adjacency matrices

Using the natural order described in the notes beside each graph, the two matrices are:
P7 graph 1 order: top-left, bottom-left, top-right, bottom-right

Tutorial 1 P8 - walks and powers of A

Claim: the number of walks of length r from vi to vj equals the (i,j) entry of A^r.
Proof idea by induction: for r = 1 this is the definition of adjacency. For r+1, every walk from vi to vj of length r+1 ends by coming from some vk adjacent to vj. Sum all length-r walks from vi to vk over possible vk; this is exactly matrix multiplication.

Tutorial 1 P9 - weighted adjacency matrices

P9 graph 1 order: top-left, middle-left, bottom-left, right-middle, right-bottom
P9 graph 2 order: top-left, bottom-left, top-right, bottom-right

Tutorial 1 P6-P8: Worked Solutions

These solutions stay inside the graph block: degree theorem, adjacency matrices and walks.

P6 - Degree theorem

Official proof idea: form the incidence matrix M with rows = vertices and columns = edges. Put M(v,e)=1 if edge e is incident with vertex v, and 0 otherwise.
Summing M by rows gives ∑v∈V deg(v). Summing M by columns gives 2 for every edge, because each undirected edge has two endpoints. Therefore ∑v∈V deg(v) = 2|E|.

P7 - Adjacency matrices

For an undirected unweighted graph, put 1 when two vertices are adjacent and 0 otherwise. The matrix must be symmetric.

P8 - Why powers of A count walks

Induction on r. For r=1, A(i,j) counts walks of length 1, because A(i,j)=1 exactly when vᵢ is adjacent to vⱼ.
Assume (Aʳ)(i,k) counts walks of length r from vᵢ to vₖ. A walk of length r+1 from vᵢ to vⱼ reaches some vₖ in r steps, then uses one edge from vₖ to vⱼ. Number of such walks = ∑ₖ(Aʳ)(i,k)A(k,j) = (Aʳ⁺¹)(i,j).
